question: One of the lessons learned from the review of Directive (EU) 2016/2102 of 26 October 2016 on the accessibility of the websites and mobile applications of public sector bodies1 (Web Accessibility Directive) is the differing interpretations of the reporting and sampling requirements across Member States.

As the review of the Web Accessibility Directive notes, one possible way of addressing these practical issues could be for the Commission and the Member States to work together on: (i) a clear reporting structure to increase the consistency of Member States’ reporting; and (ii) voluntary guidelines for Member States’ reporting on accessibility statements, feedback mechanisms and use of the disproportionate-burden clause.

This would make the monitoring exercise more efficient for reporting authorities and more consistent across countries. In addition, it would make it easier to compare results and measure progress over time. Has this joint work by the Commission and Member States already begun? If so, are there any preliminary data or conclusions?
OJ L 327, 2.12.2016, p. 1.
answer: The Commission acknowledges the importance of consistent reporting and monitoring across Member States for the effective implementation of the Web Accessibility Directive (2).

The Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/1524 establishing a monitoring methodology and the arrangements for reporting by Member States (3) already provides a common monitoring and reporting structure, aiming to facilitate consistency, without limiting innovation.

To act on the lessons learned from the review, the Commission is actively engaging with Member States through the Web Accessibility Directive Expert Group (4), which serves as a platform for exchanging best practices and addressing common issues, including the approaches to reporting and interpretability of test clauses of the Harmonised European Standard EN 301549 (5).

This dialogue is crucial in enhancing the efficiency of monitoring exercises and ensuring progress over time. There is no preliminary data or conclusions to share at present. The next Member State monitoring reports are due on 23 December 2024, and will provide further insights into implementation of the directive.

The Commission recognises the importance of digital accessibility in the broader context of the EU’s digital transformation, as reflected in the Digital Decade Policy Programme (6) and the European Accessibility Act (7). The Commission is committed to ensuring that digital technologies work for everyone, promoting inclusivity and accessibility across the EU.
